# Lab 7 assignment

## Background

Breast cancer is among the most common cancers worldwide, and for most patients it is not the primary tumour itself that is fatal, but the spread of tumour cells to distant organs (metastasis). Tumour cells can briefly acquire the ability to detach themselves from the primary tumour. They then invade surrounding tissue, enter the blood or lymphatic vessels, and finally establish new tumours in other areas of the body. Patients who develop metastasis early have a generally poorer prognosis. Therefore, it is important that we identify them at diagnosis to provide the best treatment.

How aggressively a tumour behaves depends a lot on which genes the tumour cells express and at what level. With microarray technology, we can measure the expression level of thousands of genes at the same time. This gives an expression profile for each patient, which can then be compared between groups with different clinical outcomes. Genes expressed at higher levels in one group are up-regulated, and genes expressed at lower levels are down-regulated. These genes are interesting because they can work as prognostic biomarkers.

## Aim

The aim of this analysis is to identify prognostic biomarker genes associated with early metastasis in breast cancer patients by integrating linear modeling of gene expression profiles with Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Specifically, the objectives are:

-   To fit linear models for individual gene expressions against early metastasis status, adjusting and filtering for statistically significant differentially expressed genes.

-   To perform Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using a tidyverse framework to reduce data dimensionality, evaluate variance explained by each component, and analyze patient clustering and gene loading contributions.

## Library loading

```{r}
#| message: false
library("here")
library("tidyverse") 
library("broom") 
library("cowplot")
```

## Data loading

```{r}
raw_dir <- here("data/_raw/")
data_file <- "gravier.RData"
csv_file <- "gravier.csv.gz"
data_loc <- "https://github.com/ramhiser/datamicroarray/raw/master/data/"
```

We create the path "data/\_raw/" if it doesn't exist. Here we will store our data.

```{r}
if( !dir.exists(raw_dir) ){
  dir.create(path = raw_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}
```

We download and efficiently save the dataset if absent.

```{r}
#| message: false
if( !file.exists(str_c(raw_dir, csv_file)) ){
  download.file(
    url = str_c(data_loc, data_file),
    destfile = str_c(raw_dir, data_file))
  
  load(file = str_c(raw_dir, data_file))
  write_csv(bind_cols(gravier$x, y = gravier$y), str_c(raw_dir, csv_file))
}
```

We load the data and display it.

```{r}
#| message: false
gravier <- read_csv(str_c(raw_dir, csv_file))
gravier
```

## Data Description

In this report, we look at the data from Gravier et al. (2010), who studied small node-negative breast carcinomas. The data contain log2 gene expression levels for 2,905 genes measured in 168 patients. Of these patients, 111 did not develop early metastasis, and 57 did.

## Data Processing I (linear models)

*y* is then refactored as 0/1, moved to the first column and renamed *early_metastasis*.

```{r}
gravier <- gravier |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(y = case_when(y == "poor" ~ 1,
                       y == "good" ~ 0)) |> 
  relocate(early_metastasis = y)
```

*gravier* is transformed into long format to have all genes in a single column (*gene*) and their respective expression in another (*expression*).

```{r}
gravier_long <- gravier |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -early_metastasis,
               names_to = "gene",
               values_to = "expression")
```

Fit a linear model (lm) for each gene expression using early_metastasis as the predictor. The resulting lm model is nested in *gravier_long_lms*.

```{r}
gravier_long_lms <- gravier_long |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model_object = map(.x = data, 
                       .f = ~ lm(expression ~ early_metastasis, 
                                 data = .x)
                       )
  )
```

Retrieve estimates for the slope coefficient, and tidy the model.

```{r}
gravier_estimates <- gravier_long_lms |>
  mutate(tidy_model = map (.x = model_object,
                                  .f = ~tidy(.x, conf.int = T,
                                             conf.level = 0.95)
                                  )) |>

  unnest(tidy_model) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(gene, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high)
```

compute the q.value, and the is_significant cols

```{r}
gravier_estimates <- gravier_estimates |>
  mutate(q.value = p.adjust(p.value),
       is_significant = case_when(q.value > 0.05 ~ "no", TRUE ~ "yes"))
```

## Data Processing II (PCA)

We perform PCA of the *gravier* data.

```{r}
gravier_pca <- gravier |>
  select(-early_metastasis) |>
  prcomp(scale = T)
```

We augment the data.

```{r}
gravier_pca_augmented <- gravier_pca |>
  augment(gravier |>
            select(early_metastasis)) |>
  rename_with(
    .fn = ~ str_remove(.x, "^\\.fitted"),
    .cols = starts_with(".fittedPC")
  )
```

We extract the % of explained variance by each PC from *gravier_pca*.

```{r}
gravier_pca_explained_var <- gravier_pca |>
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")
```

We extract rotations from *gravier_pca* and factor the PC column after prepending the string "PC" to each value.

```{r}
gravier_pca_rotations <- gravier_pca |>
  tidy(matrix = "rotation") |>
  mutate(PC = paste0("PC", PC) |>
           factor(levels = paste0("PC", 1:max(PC))
                 )
         ) |>
  rename(gene = column)
```

We transform the *gravier_pca_rotations* data into wide format.

```{r}
gravier_pca_rotations_wide <- gravier_pca_rotations |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = "PC",
              values_from = "value")
```

We extract the top 10 genes (greatest absolute loading) for each PC.

```{r}
top_PC_genes <- gravier_pca_rotations |>
  group_by(PC) |>
  arrange(desc(value |>
                 abs()
               )
          ) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ungroup()
```

We fit a linear model to explain each data point living in the new coordinate space by means of early_metastasis to find the most important PCs to distinguish between early metastasis or not.

```{r}
gravier_pca_coords_lms <- gravier_pca |>
  augment(gravier) |>
  select(early_metastasis, starts_with(".fittedPC")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with(".fittedPC"),
    names_to = "PC",
    values_to = "coord"
  ) |>
  group_by(PC) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model_object = map(.x = data,
                       .f = ~ lm(coord ~ early_metastasis,
                                 data = .x)
                       ),
    tidy_model = map(.x = model_object, 
                          .f = broom::tidy)
    ) |>
  unnest(tidy_model) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(p.value) |>
  mutate(PC = sub("\\.fitted", "", PC)) |>
  select(-data, -model_object, -term)
```

## Results

### Forest plot

Forest plot of significant genes by lm

```{r}
gravier_estimates |>
  filter(is_significant == "yes") |>
  mutate(gene = fct_reorder(.f = gene, .x = estimate)) |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = gene)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(x="Estimates (95%CIs)",
       y="",
       title="Genes Associated with Early Metastasis in Small Node-Negative Breast Carcinoma") +
  theme_minimal()
```

If each gene is tested on its own at a significance level of α = 0.05, we would expect around 145 genes to come out significant by chance alone. Therefore, we had to correct for multiple testing. The genes that survived the q-value assessment were retained and shown in this first plot.

The Estimates (95% CI) plot displays the average difference in gene expression between patients with early metastasis and without (reference), along with the confidence interval. This visualization highlights general trends, showing which genes appear up or down‑regulated and how wide or narrow their confidence intervals are.

### Data in PC coordinates

We perform PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the data and work with less features.

```{r}
gravier_pca_coords_lms
```

Since we want to distinguish patients with early metastasis from those without, we fitted a linear model for each PC. The results are summarised in the table above, where rows are ordered by p-value. PC4 and PC5 appear to be the most significant, and will be used in the downstream analysis.

```{r}
gravier_pca_augmented |>
  mutate(early_metastasis = factor(early_metastasis)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = PC1,
                       y = PC2,
                       colour = early_metastasis)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("1" = "steelblue", "0" = "firebrick"),
                      labels = c("1" = "No", "0" = "Yes")) +
  theme_minimal_grid(12) +
  labs(colour = "Early metastasis")
```

As a proof of concept, we visualise PC1 against PC2. The two groups are not separated in the plot. Patients with and without early metastasis lie mixed together, and neither PC1 nor PC2 tells them apart. We do see two loose clusters along PC1, but both of them contain a mix of the two groups. Therefore, the biggest differences between patients' gene expression profiles do not seem to come from metastasis status.

```{r}
gravier_pca_augmented |>
  mutate(early_metastasis = factor(early_metastasis)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = PC4,
                       y = PC5,
                       colour = early_metastasis)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("1" = "steelblue", "0" = "firebrick"),
                      labels = c("1" = "No", "0" = "Yes")) +
  theme_minimal_grid(12) +
  labs(colour = "Early metastasis")
```

There is a better separation of the two classes compared to PC1 and PC2, as expected since we selected them, but we still have some overlap, so we can't answer if the differences between patients' gene expression profiles come from the metastasis status.

### Variance explained by each PC

```{r}

gravier_pca_explained_var |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal_grid(12) +
  labs(x = "Principal Component", y = "Variance Explained")
```

PC1 covers 8.3% of the variance and PC2 covers 6.8%, so together they only give us 15.1%. After that the bars drop off slowly, and there is no clear elbow in the plot. Even though other components explain less variance than the first two, it could be interesting to consider other combinations in case another PC separates better the groups either by itself or in combination with others.

### PCA loadings

```{r}
gravier_pca_rotations |>
  filter(PC %in% paste0("PC", 1:20)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = gene, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

The following heatmap shows the gene loadings for the first 20 PCs. Certain genes drive the rotation around specific PCs, like the central dark red cluster in PC13, but overall the loadings are mildly spread across all genes. Clustering by gene loadings might help visualise which genes matter more to a PC than others.

```{r}
pcs_of_interest = c("PC4", "PC5")

target_genes <- top_PC_genes |> filter(PC %in% pcs_of_interest) |> pull(gene)

gravier_pca_rotations_wide |> filter(gene %in% target_genes) |> select(gene, all_of(pcs_of_interest))
```

Given such results, we only focused on the top 10 genes of PC4 and PC5 with the highest absolute loading.

From the two independent analyses we can see how the same genes keep popping up.

## Conclusions

Through this analysis, we identified candidate genes associated with early metastasis in breast cancer by integrating linear modeling and PCA. The linear models showed statistically significant differentially expressed genes associated with early metastasis. PCA reduced the size of the gene expression dataset, with the first two principal components explaining 15.1% of the total variance. But the PCA analysis did't show a clear separation between patients with and without early metastasis, suggesting that the main sources of variation in gene expression are not exclusively explained by the metastasis status. Finally, comparing the genes with the highest absolute loadings in the selected principal components with those identified by the linear models allowed us to investigate potential overlaps between the two approaches. These overlapping genes may represent candidate prognostic biomarkers for future investigation, although additional validation is needed to confirm their predictive value and relevance.
